stances.claim: Amicable settlement is the best way to unclog dockets -- it resolves not just the court case but, more importantly, the root causes of the dispute.
The constitutional mandate 'to settle actual controversies' encompasses both adjudication and amicable/mediated settlement -- they are both 'settling.'
stances.rhetorical_move: textual reinterpretation broadening the settlement mandate

stances.claim: Effective settlement promotion requires not just IQ and knowledge but also EQ (emotional intelligence) and LQ ('love intelligence') to read body language and parties' sincere intentions.
stances.rhetorical_move: non-cognitive skill expansion of the judicial quality criterion

stances.claim: The fear factor -- fear of being accused of bias -- must be addressed by the OCA through formulated relief from inhibitions and harassments for judges who sincerely promote settlements.
stances.rhetorical_move: institutional prescription removing a systemic barrier

notable_anecdotes: Judge Singh (now a CA justice) explaining that forging an amicable settlement 'involves attitude, knowledge and skills' -- the three-element formula that frames the author's IQ/EQ/LQ proposal.
Jesalva v. Bautista (March 24, 1959): a compromise can be effected any time -- even after judgment has been rendered and even on appeal -- the 'eureka moment' doctrine.

Judge Alaras observing that many magistrates go through pretrial 'perfunctorily' for fear of being accused of bias -- and that a disqualification or administrative charge could delay the very proceedings the settlement was meant to hasten.

Justice Romero: 'a model of humility in excellence' -- though firepower and wisdom were awesome, she shared lessons with the author when he joined the Court in 1995 that he could not have learned from school or books.
Justice Torres: despite occasional disagreements, always greeting each other with a hearty 'Kaibigan!' -- cordial professional relationship as a model for the bench.

decision_framework_signals: Pursue amicable settlement as the highest-leverage docket-unclogging tool -- it resolves root causes, not just the legal case
Add EQ and LQ to IQ as judicial selection criteria -- emotional and 'love' intelligence are as essential as legal knowledge
Use Jesalva v. Bautista as the doctrinal anchor to pursue settlement at any stage, even post-judgment
Remove the fear factor by giving judges institutional protection (OCA relief) for good-faith settlement promotion
Read counsel's pretrial position statements as settlement-sincerity signals -- even vague openness ('on acceptable terms') is actionable
one_paragraph_summary: Following reader responses to his December 24 and 31 speedy-justice columns, Panganiban endorses Judge Soliman Santos Jr.'s (RTC Naga) proposal that amicable settlement is the best way to unclog the courts' 980,000 pending cases -- noting the constitutional mandate for courts 'to settle actual controversies' covers both adjudication and mediated settlement. RA 9285, the Civil Code, the Rules of Court, and SC circulars all encourage such settlements, which resolve the root causes of disputes rather than just the court case. The barrier is not law but attitude: citing Justice Maria Filomena Singh's framework, the author argues that settlement requires not just IQ and skills (learnable from books) but also EQ (emotional intelligence) and LQ ('love intelligence') -- reading body language, pretrial briefs, and counsel positions to identify sincere settlement intent. Jesalva v. Bautista (March 24, 1959) authorizes settlement any time, even after judgment on appeal. The other barrier is the fear factor, flagged by Judge Selma Alaras: many judges go through pretrial 'perfunctorily' because a party may interpret settlement pressure as bias, leading to disqualification requests or administrative charges. The OCA should formulate immediate relief from inhibitions and harassments for judges who sincerely promote settlements. The column closes with tributes to two recently deceased jurists: Justice Flerida Ruth Romero -- 'a model of humility in excellence' who generously shared lessons with the author when he joined the Court in 1995, eulogized by CJ Davide as a jurist of 'proven integrity, competence, independence and courage' -- and Justice Justo Torres, with whom the author occasionally disagreed but always exchanged a hearty 'Kaibigan!' greeting.
